openers.jurassic-period: The Jurassic begins with the land drying out and the dinosaurs moving in. As Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried, the great Pangean megamonsoon began to fall apart, and the Farallon plate started sinking beneath western North America as Pangaea broke up. With their reptile rivals gone after the end-Triassic extinction, dinosaurs surged in diversity and abundance, and the first definitive ornithischians appeared. In the sea, ammonoids that had nearly vanished radiated into the ammonites proper, and plesiosaurs were already richly varied. Even the amphibians changed, as the first modern frogs and salamanders began to diversify.
openers.early-jurassic-epoch: In the wreckage of the end-Triassic extinction, the Early Jurassic rebuilt fast. British seafloor communities began recovering almost at once, despite repeated relapses into anoxia, and ammonites and neoselachian sharks radiated through the seas. On land, dinosaurs surged into the space left by vanished rivals, crocodylomorphs found new niches, and the first definitive ornithischians appeared. Plant life turned over too: conifers replaced the hot fernlands of China's Sichuan Basin, while Dicroidium lingered only in Antarctica. Even ocean chemistry shifted, from aragonite seas to calcite seas.

reviews.late-triassic-epoch: The Late Triassic began with a climate shock and ended with a catastrophe. The Wrangellia eruptions brought the Carnian rains, and in that wet spell dinosaurs, lepidosaurs and new plankton diversified while ammonoids and crinoids suffered. Through the Norian, dinosaurs, pterosaurs, the first true turtles and mammaliaforms spread, even as crurotarsans still held more niches and impacts such as Manicouagan struck. Then the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupted in brief, violent pulses, and the End-Triassic Thermal Event, acidified oceans and anoxia followed. The resulting mass extinction removed the crurotarsans and many other groups, leaving the land to the dinosaurs.
reviews.jurassic-period: Two quiet trends frame the Jurassic. As the continents drifted apart, the Pangean megamonsoon that had driven Triassic weather kept weakening, and Gondwana and southern Laurasia dried out. Among the animals, the old temnospondyls faded to a single surviving group, the brachyopoids. In their place the lissamphibians began to diversify, giving rise to the first modern frogs and salamanders.

tria-079.title: The last rhynchosaurs vanish
tria-079.text: Once among the most abundant plant-eaters on Earth, the beaked hyperodapedontine rhynchosaurs died out in the early Norian. Brazil's Teyumbaita is the only rhynchosaur known with confidence to have survived into that age. The exact date of their end is uncertain. They lasted at least into the early to middle Norian, though one suggestion places their extinction in an end-Carnian crisis instead.

tria-080.title: A mid-Norian die-off strikes the seas
tria-080.text: Single-celled radiolarians, sponges, eel-like conodonts and Triassic ammonoids all took losses in the middle of the Norian. This marine extinction has been blamed on {{ref:tria-090}}. That impact may also have hastened the slide of conodonts and ammonoids toward their final end-Triassic extinction.

tria-082.title: Sea level sinks to a Rhaetian low
tria-082.text: From a Carnian high of up to 50 m above today's level, the sea began to retreat in the Norian. It bottomed out about 50 m below present in the mid-Rhaetian, and low levels lasted into the earliest Jurassic. Ice cannot explain the swing, because there is no evidence of Triassic ice sheets. At the very end of the Triassic, the sea flooded most of central and western Europe, turning it into an archipelago. A drop in sea level seen in Europe and the Middle East at the extinction now looks regional rather than global.

tria-084.title: Mammaliaforms, the closest kin of mammals, appear
tria-084.text:
Tiny, nocturnal and warm-blooded, the first mammaliaforms lived in the shadow of the dinosaurs. Mammaliaforms are mammals plus their closest extinct kin, and they arose from advanced probainognathian cynodonts in the Late Triassic. Exactly when is still argued. Some studies place their origin in the Carnian pluvial episode, others in the Norian or at the very end of the Triassic.

Unambiguous forms such as morganucodonts and haramiyids appeared in the Norian across Europe and Greenland, as probainognathians became prominent. Older claims look shaky. Tikitherium may be a misidentified Cenozoic shrew, and Adelobasileus is no older than 225 million years. These early animals were small, mostly insect-eating, and their bodies were already changing: bones of the old jaw were moving into the middle ear. Cynodonts were the only therapsids to outlast the Triassic, and mammaliaforms went on to diversify widely in the Jurassic.

tria-083.title: A cooler spell follows the Carnian heat
tria-083.text: After the Carnian's rains and warmth, the climate turned cooler. The Early Norian Cool Interval lasted from about 227 to 217 million years ago, following the Mid-Carnian Warm Interval that the Carnian pluvial episode had brought. At the Carnian–Norian boundary, a positive carbon-isotope excursion, a shift toward heavier carbon, suggests more organic carbon was being buried.

tria-085.title: Teleosts, today's dominant fishes, first appear
tria-085.text: More than 99% of living ray-finned fishes are teleosts, and the group first appears around 225 million years ago. Early stem teleosts such as Prohalecites swam in the western Tethys. From those modest beginnings came the fishes that now dominate rivers, lakes and oceans worldwide.

tria-089.title: Warmth returns, and Pangaea turns swampy
tria-089.text: Earth's orbit helped turn deserts into swamps. Warmer conditions, the Mid-Norian Warm Interval, lasted from about 217 to 209 million years ago. Around 214 million years ago a brief cooling interrupted it, possibly linked to the Manicouagan impact. Around 212 million years ago, a peak in orbital eccentricity, the stretching of Earth's path around the Sun, made much of Pangaea swampy and shrank its arid zones.

tria-090.title: An asteroid 5 km wide blasts out Manicouagan
tria-090.text: Shocked quartz from a single strike in Quebec turns up as far away as England and Japan. An asteroid about 5 km wide hit there, excavating a multiple-ring crater about 100 km across, among the largest on Earth. Of all Mesozoic impacts, only Chicxulub was bigger. It may have caused a brief cooling, a mid-Norian marine extinction and the Adamanian–Revueltian turnover on land, but direct evidence is lacking. Some 13 million years older than the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, it is no longer thought to have caused the end-Triassic extinction.

tria-091.title: A turnover reshapes Southwest faunas
tria-091.text: In the rocks of the Chinle Formation, several land animals vanish quickly around 215 million years ago. Trilophosaurus, Desmatosuchus, dicynodonts and many phytosaurs disappeared from the American Southwest, and new aetosaurs and phytosaurs replaced them. Pollen shifted to dry-adapted plants, suggesting rising aridity, and the Manicouagan impact is one proposed cause. Both the cause and the importance of this turnover are debated. It may have been only a small, local extinction.

tria-092.title: Argoland begins to splinter off Australia
tria-092.text: Gondwana started shedding pieces. Around 215 million years ago, Argoland, on Australia's northern margin, began breaking into microcontinental fragments. It happened during Late Triassic rifting that pulled the Lhasa terrane away from Gondwana. A major Norian rifting episode, about 210 million years ago, split Gondwana in two parts.

tria-093.title: Proganochelys completes the turtle shell
tria-093.text: The turtle shell took millions of years to finish. In the Norian, the earliest true turtles appeared, among them Proganochelys and Proterochersis. Proganochelys completed what {{ref:tria-044}} had begun, with a fully developed carapace and plastron. Side-necked and hidden-necked turtles, the two lines that include all living turtles, are estimated to have split about 210 million years ago.

tria-094.title: Early dinosaur rivals vanish in the mid-Norian
tria-094.text: The dinosaurs' rise owed something to their rivals' bad luck. About 215 million years ago, a range of basal archosauromorphs, early-branching archosaur relatives including the protorosaurs, died out. It was the first of two Triassic extinctions that removed most of the early dinosaurs' competitors. Early dinosaur lineages diversified through the Carnian and Norian, possibly filling the emptied niches.

tria-095.title: A cool Rhaetian ends in extreme heat
tria-095.text: The Triassic's last cool spell ended in a furnace. A cooler phase, the Rhaetian Cool Interval, lasted from about 209 to 201 million years ago. Then an extreme warming, the {{ref:tria-103}}, closed the period, and it is blamed for the mass extinction.

tria-096.title: An asteroid strikes an island in western France
tria-096.text: Near Limoges, an asteroid hit an island on the edge of the Massif Central, close to the sea. It left the Rochechouart structure, about 23 km across, and probably raised a large tsunami. Its age has long been debated, with estimates from under 150 to over 240 million years, but recent dates converge on 203–207 million years ago. That puts it a few million years before the Triassic–Jurassic boundary. Even so, it seems too small to have caused the mass extinction.

tria-097.title: The giant shastasaurs vanish from the seas
tria-097.text: Shonisaurus grew to 15 m long, one of the shastasaurian ichthyosaurs that reached huge sizes in the Carnian and Norian. These giants seem to have vanished at the end of the Norian, as ichthyosaur variety declined. Growing competition from sharks, teleost fishes and the first plesiosaurs may explain the decline.

tria-099.title: A disputed die-off at the Norian–Rhaetian boundary
tria-099.text: Monotis, a large bivalve once found worldwide, lost almost all its species. Its last shells lie between ash beds dated 205.70 and 205.30 million years old. The same extinction near the Norian–Rhaetian boundary hit ammonoids, other bivalves, conodonts and radiolarians, and a sharp negative carbon-isotope spike is tied to it. Alaska's Angayucham large igneous province or the Rochechouart impact may have caused it. Yet one source calls it an alleged, much smaller event, and its dating and effects remain uncertain.

tria-098.title: Marine life falters before the final crisis
tria-098.text: Mean annual temperatures rose 7–9 °C from the late Norian into the Rhaetian. The seas were already in trouble. Gastropods, or snails, suffered steady losses through the late Norian and Rhaetian, and offshore bryozoans had been declining since the Norian. Anoxia struck northeastern Panthalassa during the Rhaetian, and the carbon cycle was disturbed before the main crisis began.

tria-100.title: The Karoo igneous province stirs
tria-100.text: A volcanic giant began to wake on the northern edge of what is now southern Africa's Karoo. Igneous activity of the Karoo large igneous province started about 204 million years ago on its northern margin. Its later Karoo-Ferrar flood basalts are tied to the Toarcian extinction of the Early Jurassic.

tria-101.title: Plesiosaurs appear at the end of the Triassic
tria-101.text: Of all the flipper-limbed sauropterygians, only one branch survived the end of the Triassic, and it had only just arrived. Plesiosaurs first appeared in the latest Triassic, possibly in the Rhaetian, about 203 million years ago. At least six plesiosaur lineages crossed into the Jurassic, while every other sauropterygian died out. They became especially common in the Jurassic and lasted until the end-Cretaceous extinction.

tria-102.title: The Central Atlantic magmatic province erupts
tria-102.text:
Lava covered about 11 million km² across four continents. As central Pangaea rifted, the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, or CAMP, built Earth's largest continental igneous province, with 2–6 million km³ of lava. The first lavas date to 201.566 ± 0.031 million years ago and the last to 201.36 ± 0.02 million years ago.

The eruptions came in four main pulses. Each lasted no more than about 100 years, and together they were spread over some 600,000 years. Large bodies of magma had built up about 100,000 years before the eruptions began. CAMP ended the long rifting of the Central Atlantic. It is widely blamed for the Triassic–Jurassic extinction, a link that became firmer in 2013.

tria-103.title: Volcanic carbon drives an extreme end-Triassic warming
tria-103.text: Tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide, trapped in CAMP basalts, hold the smoking gun. They show the volcanism helped trigger the End-Triassic Thermal Event, an extreme warming at the very end of the Triassic that drove the mass extinction. The pulses released their carbon over mere centuries, a pace that invites comparison with today's human-caused warming. Longer-term warming and ocean acidification followed the eruptions. A thermal spike marks the start of the Jurassic.

tria-104.title: The end-Triassic extinction hands the land to dinosaurs
tria-104.text:
About 46–72% of marine genera disappeared. One of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions ended the Triassic 201.4 million years ago, driven by CAMP volcanism and the warming it caused. In the sea, ammonites were nearly wiped out, conodonts vanished and reefs collapsed, completing the oceans' shift to the modern evolutionary fauna.

On land, most archosaurs died out except crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs, along with most therapsids and large amphibians. One estimate puts tetrapod losses at 42%. Plants turned over too, with 17–73% of Rhaetian plants lost by various estimates, though some researchers see a restructuring rather than a plant mass extinction. The crisis removed the crurotarsans, the dinosaurs' main rivals. That opening let dinosaurs dominate the Jurassic.

tria-105.title: Oceans lose their oxygen and turn acidic
tria-105.text: Misshapen nannoplankton tell of seas turned corrosive. Black shales and a sharp negative uranium-isotope shift show that ocean oxygen fell steeply during the extinction. Anoxia reached the western and eastern Tethys and Panthalassa and lasted into the Hettangian, as nutrients from the land fed the seas. Green sulfur bacteria, which photosynthesize with hydrogen sulfide, grew markedly across the boundary. A worldwide pause in carbonate deposition adds to the evidence of severe acidification. This is the best-established case of acidification causing a marine mass extinction, selectively killing organisms with thick skeletons of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.

tria-108.title: The last dicynodonts disappear
tria-108.text: The group of Lystrosaurus had a long run. Dicynodonts were among the most successful therapsids of the Permian and stayed large plant-eaters until they died out at the end of the Triassic. Their last appearance is uncertain. They survived at least into the late Norian or earliest Rhaetian.

tria-110.title: Phytosaurs, aetosaurs and rauisuchians die out
tria-110.text: The crocodile line ruled much of the Late Triassic, and almost all of it was lost at once. Phytosaurs and aetosaurs, common in Late Triassic faunas, were completely wiped out by the end-Triassic extinction. Among the pseudosuchians, only small crocodylomorphs survived. Plant-eaters like aetosaurs and the meat-eating rauisuchids died out. The timing is hard to pin down, because the Rhaetian and Hettangian hold few large land animals and some groups may have vanished earlier.

jura-019.title: Modern amphibians branch out: the first frogs and salamanders
jura-019.text: Every frog and salamander alive today belongs to a lineage that began spreading out in the Jurassic. Lissamphibians, the modern amphibians, diversified then, producing the first modern frogs and salamanders. Eocaecilia, a stem relative of today's limbless caecilians, already lived in Early Jurassic Arizona. Stem-frogs and the extinct albanerpetontids followed in the Middle Jurassic. Meanwhile the old guard faded. Of the once-diverse temnospondyls, only the brachyopoids survived into the Jurassic.

jura-026.title: Pangaea's great monsoon starts to fail
jura-026.text: The rains that had swept Pangaea for an entire period began to fail. At the start of the Jurassic, the Pangean megamonsoon started falling apart. Gondwana, the southern half of Pangaea, dried out, and so did southern Laurasia. As the continents drifted apart, the monsoon kept weakening through the rest of the Jurassic.
